subproblem.title: Compact inner approximation of W ∩ E inside an open W ⊆ U for a measure finite on compact subsets of U
subproblem.statement: Let P ∈ ℕ, U ⊆ ℝ^P, and μ a measure on the Borel sets of ℝ^P with μ(K) < ∞ for every compact K ⊆ U. Let E ⊆ ℝ^P be Borel, W ⊆ U open and c ∈ [0, ∞] with c < μ(W ∩ E). Then there is a compact set K ⊆ W ∩ E with c < μ(K).
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P : ℕ) (U : Set (Eucl P)) (μ : Measure (Eucl P)), (∀ K : Set (Eucl P), IsCompact K → K ⊆ U → μ K < ∞) → ∀ E : Set (Eucl P), MeasurableSet E → ∀ W : Set (Eucl P), IsOpen W → W ⊆ U → ∀ c : ℝ≥0∞, c < μ (W ∩ E) → ∃ K : Set (Eucl P), IsCompact K ∧ K ⊆ W ∩ E ∧ c < μ K
subproblem.natural_proof:
Conventions. ℝ^P = Eucl P = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin P) with its Euclidean metric and Borel σ-algebra; μ is a measure on this σ-algebra and all measure values lie in [0, ∞]. For S ⊆ ℝ^P and δ > 0, thickening(δ, S) = {x : ∃ y ∈ S, dist(x, y) < δ}, an open set. Source: Simon, Introduction to GMT, Ch. 6, 2.7–2.9 (pp. 136–137). This argument is steps 2–4 of the supplied proof of the parent theorem smr_ufd_compact_lusin_set (step U3 of smr_exists_unit_form_gt), extracted with the details filled in. Step 1 of the parent proof (finiteness of c) is not needed here.

1. (Compact exhaustion of W.) For j ∈ ℕ put F_j := ℝ^P ∖ thickening(1/(j+1), ℝ^P ∖ W) and K_j := closedBall(0, j) ∩ F_j = closedBall(0, j) ∖ thickening(1/(j+1), ℝ^P ∖ W).
 (a) K_j is compact. F_j is closed (the complement of an open set), so K_j is a closed subset of closedBall(0, j). That ball is compact because ℝ^P is a proper metric space.
 (b) K_j ⊆ W. If x ∉ W, then x ∈ ℝ^P ∖ W ⊆ thickening(1/(j+1), ℝ^P ∖ W) (take y := x), so x ∉ F_j ⊇ K_j.
 (c) K_i ⊆ K_j for i ≤ j. First, closedBall(0, i) ⊆ closedBall(0, j). Second, 1/(j+1) ≤ 1/(i+1), so thickening(1/(j+1), ℝ^P ∖ W) ⊆ thickening(1/(i+1), ℝ^P ∖ W), hence F_i ⊆ F_j.
 (d) ⋃_j K_j = W. "⊆" is (b). Conversely, let x ∈ W. As W is open, there is r > 0 with ball(x, r) ⊆ W. Choose j ∈ ℕ with j ≥ ‖x‖ and 1/(j+1) ≤ r. If y ∉ W, then y ∉ ball(x, r), so dist(x, y) ≥ r ≥ 1/(j+1). Hence x ∉ thickening(1/(j+1), ℝ^P ∖ W), i.e. x ∈ F_j. Also ‖x‖ ≤ j, i.e. x ∈ closedBall(0, j). So x ∈ K_j.
 (e) μ(K_j) < ∞ for every j: K_j is compact by (a) and K_j ⊆ W ⊆ U by (b), so the hypothesis applies.
 (Variant: any increasing sequence of closed sets F_j ⊆ W with ⋃_j F_j = W may replace the F_j above, for example the sequence given by Mathlib's IsOpen.exists_iUnion_isClosed. Then K_j := F_j ∩ closedBall(0, j) satisfies (a)–(e) by the same arguments. In (d), pick i with x ∈ F_i, take j ≥ max(i, ‖x‖), and use F_i ⊆ F_j.)
2. (Continuity from below.) The sets E ∩ K_j (j ∈ ℕ) are Borel, since E is Borel and K_j is closed. They increase with j by 1(c), and ⋃_j (E ∩ K_j) = E ∩ ⋃_j K_j = E ∩ W = W ∩ E by 1(d). By continuity of measures along increasing sequences, μ(E ∩ K_j) → μ(W ∩ E) as j → ∞. Since c < μ(W ∩ E), the open neighbourhood (c, ∞] of the limit contains μ(E ∩ K_j) for all large j. Fix one such j, so that c < μ(E ∩ K_j), and put E′ := E ∩ K_j.
3. (A Borel piece of finite measure.) E′ is Borel and E′ ⊆ E ∩ W by 1(b). Also μ(E′) ≤ μ(K_j) < ∞ by monotonicity and 1(e).
4. (Inner regularity by compact sets.) Every measure on ℝ^P is inner regular by compact sets on Borel sets of finite measure: if S ⊆ ℝ^P is Borel with μ(S) < ∞ and r < μ(S), then some compact K ⊆ S has r < μ(K).
 Justification: ν(B) := μ(B ∩ S) defines a finite Borel measure on the complete separable metric space ℝ^P. Finite Borel measures on such spaces are inner regular by compact sets on all Borel sets (Ulam's theorem). On ℝ^P this also follows directly: approximate from inside by closed sets, which works for finite Borel measures on metric spaces, then intersect with large closed balls, using that ν is finite. Hence ν(S) = sup{ν(K) : K ⊆ S compact}. Since ν(S) = μ(S) > r, some compact K ⊆ S has r < ν(K) = μ(K ∩ S) = μ(K).
 In Mathlib this is the instance instInnerRegularCompactLTTopOfIsCompletelyPseudoMetrizableSpace (Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/RegularityCompacts.lean) together with MeasurableSet.exists_lt_isCompact_of_ne_top (Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/Regular.lean).
 Apply this with S := E′ and r := c, which steps 2 and 3 allow. This gives a compact K ⊆ E′ with c < μ(K).
5. (Conclusion.) K is compact, K ⊆ E′ ⊆ E ∩ W = W ∩ E by step 3, and c < μ(K). ∎

Formalization note (not part of the argument): GMT.Ch06.Submission does not import the step-4 instance for an arbitrary μ. There are two options, both checked to compile with the frozen submission:
- add `import Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Measure.RegularityCompacts` and use MeasurableSet.exists_lt_isCompact_of_ne_top directly;
- with the base imports only, apply MeasurableSet.exists_lt_isCompact_of_ne_top to the finite measure μ.restrict E′ (using `Fact (μ E′ < ∞)` and Measure.restrict_apply_self), then transfer back with Measure.restrict_eq_self.
Useful names: IsOpen.exists_iUnion_isClosed, isCompact_closedBall, IsCompact.inter_left, tendsto_measure_iUnion_atTop, tendsto_order, Filter.Eventually.exists. A scratch proof along steps 1–5, using the IsOpen.exists_iUnion_isClosed variant of step 1, compiles with axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound].
proof_key_steps: Compact exhaustion of W: K_j := closedBall(0, j) ∖ thickening(1/(j+1), ℝ^P ∖ W). These are compact, increasing, contained in W, with ⋃_j K_j = W, and μ(K_j) < ∞ because K_j ⊆ W ⊆ U.
Continuity from below: μ(E ∩ K_j) → μ(W ∩ E) > c, so some j has c < μ(E′) for the Borel set E′ := E ∩ K_j.
Finiteness: μ(E′) ≤ μ(K_j) < ∞, and E′ ⊆ W ∩ E.
Inner regularity by compact sets on finite-measure Borel sets of the Polish space ℝ^P (InnerRegularCompactLTTop; MeasurableSet.exists_lt_isCompact_of_ne_top) gives a compact K ⊆ E′ with c < μ(K).
Hence K is compact, K ⊆ W ∩ E and c < μ(K).

subproblem.title: Lusin's theorem with compact sets for Borel maps ℝ^P → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N) and an arbitrary measure on a finite-measure Borel set
subproblem.statement: Let P, N ∈ ℕ, μ a measure on the Borel sets of ℝ^P, and u : ℝ^P → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N) Borel. Let A ⊆ ℝ^P be Borel with μ(A) < ∞ and let ε ∈ (0, ∞]. Then there is a compact set C ⊆ A with μ(A ∖ C) < ε such that u is continuous on C.
subproblem.lean_statement: ∀ (P N : ℕ) (μ : Measure (Eucl P)) (u : Eucl P → EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N)), Measurable u → ∀ A : Set (Eucl P), MeasurableSet A → μ A ≠ ∞ → ∀ ε : ℝ≥0∞, ε ≠ 0 → ∃ C : Set (Eucl P), IsCompact C ∧ C ⊆ A ∧ μ (A \ C) < ε ∧ ContinuousOn u C
subproblem.natural_proof:
Conventions. ℝ^P = Eucl P = EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin P) with its Euclidean metric and Borel σ-algebra; μ is a measure on this σ-algebra; measure values, ε and η lie in [0, ∞]. H := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin N). For a ∈ H and i ∈ Fin N, the coordinate is a_i = ⟨a, e_i⟩, where e_i = EuclideanSpace.single i 1 is the standard basis.

Source: Simon, Introduction to GMT, Ch. 1, 1.17 (Lusin's theorem), applied coordinatewise. This argument is steps 4(b), 5, 6 and 7 of the supplied proof of the parent theorem smr_ufd_compact_lusin_set (step U4 of smr_exists_unit_form_gt). It is extracted with one change: the compact set C₀ there is replaced by an arbitrary Borel set A of finite measure, and one extra compact approximation K of A (step 5) restores compactness.

1. (Closed and compact inner approximation.) For every Borel S ⊆ ℝ^P with μ(S) < ∞ and every δ ∈ (0, ∞], there is a compact, hence closed, F ⊆ S with μ(S ∖ F) < δ.
 Proof: if μ(S) < δ, take F := ∅. Otherwise 0 < δ ≤ μ(S) < ∞, so μ(S) − δ < μ(S).
 Every measure on ℝ^P is inner regular by compact sets on Borel sets of finite measure. Justification: ν(B) := μ(B ∩ S) is a finite Borel measure on the complete separable metric space ℝ^P, hence inner regular by compact sets (Ulam's theorem), and ν(K) = μ(K) for K ⊆ S. In Mathlib this is the instance instInnerRegularCompactLTTopOfIsCompletelyPseudoMetrizableSpace.
 So there is a compact F ⊆ S with μ(S) − δ < μ(F). F is closed because ℝ^P is Hausdorff, hence F is Borel. Since μ(F) ≤ μ(S) < ∞, we get μ(S ∖ F) = μ(S) − μ(F) < δ. In Mathlib this is MeasurableSet.exists_isCompact_isClosed_sdiff_lt.
2. (Error budget.) Since ε ≠ 0 and N + 1 ≠ ∞, there is η ∈ [0, ∞] with 0 < η and (N + 1)·η < ε (for example via ENNReal.exists_pos_mul_lt). Then η < ∞: η = ∞ would give (N + 1)·η = ∞ < ε, which is impossible.
3. (Coordinates are Borel.) For i ∈ Fin N let u_i : ℝ^P → ℝ, u_i(x) := u(x)_i. The coordinate map H → ℝ, a ↦ a_i, is linear on a finite-dimensional space, hence continuous (EuclideanSpace.proj i) and Borel. So u_i, its composition with the Borel map u, is Borel.
4. (Lusin's theorem for each coordinate.) Lusin's theorem is available as Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.exists_isClosed_continuousOn_of_measurable (Simon Ch. 1, 1.17). Its setting: ν is a measure on a topological space X whose open sets are measurable, satisfying the closed-regularity hypothesis "for every measurable S with ν(S) ≠ ∞ and every δ ≠ 0 there is a closed F ⊆ S with ν(S ∖ F) < δ". Its conclusion: for every measurable A with ν(A) ≠ ∞, every measurable f : X → ℝ and every ε′ ≠ 0, there is a closed C ⊆ A with ν(A ∖ C) < ε′ such that f is continuous on C.
 For X = ℝ^P (Borel σ-algebra) and ν = μ, the hypothesis holds by step 1. For each i ∈ Fin N, apply the theorem to A (Borel, μ(A) ≠ ∞), f := u_i (Borel by step 3) and ε′ := η ≠ 0. This gives a closed F_i ⊆ A with μ(A ∖ F_i) < η such that u_i is continuous on F_i.
5. (A compact piece of A.) Step 1 with S := A and δ := η gives a compact K ⊆ A with μ(A ∖ K) < η.
6. (The set C.) Put C := K ∩ ⋂_{i ∈ Fin N} F_i (so C = K when N = 0). Every F_i is closed, so ⋂_i F_i is closed. C is the intersection of the compact set K with a closed set, hence compact. Moreover C ⊆ K ⊆ A.
7. (u is continuous on C.) For each i ∈ Fin N we have C ⊆ F_i, so u_i is continuous on C. A map into the finite product ℝ^{Fin N} is continuous on C iff each coordinate is (continuousOn_pi), so x ↦ (u_i(x))_{i ∈ Fin N} is continuous on C. Now u(x) is the image of (u_i(x))_i under the identification ℝ^{Fin N} → H (WithLp.toLp 2). That identification is a linear bijection between finite-dimensional spaces, hence continuous (PiLp.continuous_toLp). So the composition u is continuous on C.
8. (Measure of A ∖ C.) Let x ∈ A ∖ C. If x ∉ K, then x ∈ A ∖ K. If x ∈ K, then x ∉ ⋂_i F_i, so x ∉ F_i for some i, and x ∈ A ∖ F_i. Hence A ∖ C ⊆ (A ∖ K) ∪ ⋃_{i ∈ Fin N} (A ∖ F_i). By monotonicity and finite subadditivity, μ(A ∖ C) ≤ μ(A ∖ K) + Σ_{i ∈ Fin N} μ(A ∖ F_i).
 By step 4, Σ_i μ(A ∖ F_i) ≤ Σ_i η = N·η, which is finite by step 2. Together with μ(A ∖ K) < η (step 5), this gives μ(A ∖ C) < η + N·η = (N + 1)·η < ε by step 2.
9. (Conclusion.) C is compact, C ⊆ A, μ(A ∖ C) < ε, and u is continuous on C. ∎

Formalization note (not part of the argument): GMT.Ch06.Submission imports neither of the following, and adding both was checked to compile with the frozen submission:
- `import Poincare.SimonGMT.Chapter01.Lusin`, for SimonGMT's Lusin theorem;
- `import Mathlib.MeasureTheory.Measure.RegularityCompacts`, for the step-1 instance with an arbitrary μ.

- Continuity: continuousOn_pi on fun x => WithLp.ofLp (u x), then (PiLp.continuous_toLp 2 _).comp_continuousOn.
A scratch proof along steps 1–9 compiles with axioms [propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound].
proof_key_steps: Regularity: each Borel S with μ(S) < ∞ has, for every δ > 0, a compact (hence closed) F ⊆ S with μ(S ∖ F) < δ (InnerRegularCompactLTTop on ℝ^P; MeasurableSet.exists_isCompact_isClosed_sdiff_lt).
Error budget: choose η ∈ (0, ∞) with (N + 1)·η < ε.

Each coordinate u_i is Borel. SimonGMT Lusin (Ch. 1, 1.17), with its closed-regularity hypothesis supplied by the regularity step, gives a closed F_i ⊆ A with μ(A ∖ F_i) < η on which u_i is continuous.
Take a compact K ⊆ A with μ(A ∖ K) < η. Then C := K ∩ ⋂_i F_i is compact and C ⊆ A.
u is continuous on C because all its coordinates are (continuousOn_pi, PiLp.continuous_toLp).
A ∖ C ⊆ (A ∖ K) ∪ ⋃_i (A ∖ F_i), so μ(A ∖ C) < η + N·η = (N + 1)·η < ε.

The proof independently supplies Lusin's full closed-regularity hypothesis, obtains measurable coordinates, and correctly transfers coordinate continuity through PiLp. Intersecting with K ensures compactness, including N = 0. Positive finite η makes the strict finite-sum estimate valid, also for ε = ∞. No unstated measure assumption or circular dependency is used; the supplied proof is complete.
